title: High Parallel Complexity Graphs and Memory-Hard Functions

findings.claim: Cumulative pebbling complexity (memory summed over time) captures parallel cost where older pebbling measures fail.
findings.quote: cumulative complexity (CC) and show how it overcomes a crucial shortcoming in the parallel setting exhibited by more traditional complexity measures used in past reductions.
findings.bears_on: Depth-robust-graph arguments from memory-hard functions are a route to NCI-style bounds for computations whose dependency DAG is depth-robust, as sequential SGD's may be.

title: Minimizing Communication in Linear Algebra
authors: Grey Ballard, James Demmel, Olga Holtz, Oded Schwartz

findings.claim: For a large class of direct linear algebra, communication is at least the arithmetic count divided by the square root of the fast (or local) memory size.
findings.quote: In both cases the lower bound may be expressed as $\Omega$(#arithmetic operations / $\sqrt{M}$), where $M$ is the size of the fast memory (or local memory in the parallel case).

quantities.condition: communication >= (#arithmetic operations) / M^0.5; Loomis-Whitney segment argument

findings.bears_on: The segment argument (bound work per segment of M loads, divide total work by it) is exactly how an NCI slowdown bound is built: bound useful training progress per block given K novel bits, then count blocks.

findings.claim: Within a segment, the number of multiply-adds is bounded by the geometric mean of the three operand projections (Loomis-Whitney).
findings.quote: Let $|\cdot|$ denote the cardinality of a set. Then $|V|\leq\sqrt{|A_{x}|\cdot|A_{y}|\cdot|A_{z}|}$.
findings.bears_on: With committed weights free, one projection is unbounded and NCI does not cap outputs, so this inequality degenerates to a bound linear in the novel input; NCI's bounds must come from dependency structure instead.

findings.claim: Operands created and discarded inside a segment cannot be bounded by the segment argument without extra structure.
findings.quote: The S2/D2 operands, those created during the segment and then discarded without causing any slow memory traffic, cannot be bounded without further information.
findings.bears_on: Matches NCI's setting in which intermediates inside a Gamma-gate block are free; NCI bounds cannot rely on charging for in-block intermediates.

title: Graph Expansion and Communication Costs of Fast Matrix Multiplication
authors: Grey Ballard, James Demmel, Olga Holtz, Oded Schwartz
venue: Journal of the ACM 59(6) (SPAA 2011 best paper; arXiv 1109.1693)

findings.claim: Communication cost is governed by the edge expansion of the computation graph.
findings.quote: The communication cost of algorithms (also known as I/O-complexity) is shown to be closely related to the expansion properties of the corresponding computation graphs.
findings.bears_on: Expansion of the training circuit's DAG (how many edges leave any small set of gates) is a candidate route to NCI bounds that survive restructuring of matrix products.

findings.claim: Strassen-like algorithms need Omega((n/sqrt(M))^omega0 * M) communication, p times less with p processors.
findings.quote: where $\omega_{0}$ is the exponent in the arithmetic count (e.g., $\omega_{0}=\lg 7$ for Strassen, and $\omega_{0}=3$ for conventional matrix multiplication). With $p$ parallel processors, each with fast memory of size $M$, the lower bound is $p$ times smaller.

quantities.condition: derived: lg 7 = 2.807 for Strassen; omega0 = 3 for conventional

findings.bears_on: Shows how to extend a per-piece bound to fast bilinear algorithms; an NCI bound on matrix-product-heavy training should hold for any bilinear restructuring an adversary might choose.

findings.claim: The expansion approach forbids recomputation, a serious gap for NCI where a block has Gamma gates to recompute freely.
findings.quote: We were not able to allow recomputation using our edge expansion approach.
findings.bears_on: Expansion bounds cannot be imported into NCI as is; NCI must allow recomputation, which pushes toward the Grigoriev-flow (Bilardi-De Stefani) or communication-complexity (Saha-Ye) techniques.

findings.claim: Loomis-Whitney counting fails once an algorithm uses distributivity, as Strassen's does.
findings.quote: approach, however, is not suitable when distributivity is used, as is the case in Strassen
findings.bears_on: Geometric counting of products is not robust to algebraic restructuring; NCI proofs should not depend on the circuit computing matrix products the classical way.

title: Communication Steps for Parallel Query Processing
authors: Paul Beame, Paraschos Koutris, Dan Suciu

findings.claim: In the MPC model each server receives O(n/p^(1-epsilon)) bits per round, epsilon controlling replication; one-round evaluation of a query q needs epsilon >= 1 - 1/tau*.
findings.quote: we show that any algorithm requires ε ≥ 1--1/τ*, where τ* is the fractional vertex cover of the hypergraph of q
findings.bears_on: Replication-based lower bounds charge for copying input data; NCI does not charge for committed data, so the analogous NCI bound must charge only computed data that crosses blocks.

findings.claim: With near-linear per-processor load, Omega(log p) rounds are needed for some queries.
findings.quote: per-processor load that is O (m/p 1-ε ) requires Ω(log p) rounds of communication.
findings.bears_on: Round-versus-load tradeoffs correspond to NCI's depth-versus-K tradeoff: a smaller K forces a longer chain of dependent blocks.

title: Logical Depth and Physical Complexity
venue: The Universal Turing Machine: A Half-Century Survey (ed. R. Herken), Oxford University Press

findings.claim: Logical depth is the time a universal machine needs to produce an object from an algorithmically random input.
findings.quote: defining an object’s “logical depth” as the time required by a standard universal Turing machine to gen erate it from an input that is algorithmically random
findings.bears_on: Trained weights are deep objects in Bennett's sense; NCI targets the accumulation of depth (training) while letting shallow, prompt-driven computation (inference) through.

findings.claim: Depth obeys a slow-growth law: deep objects cannot be produced quickly from shallow ones.
findings.quote: slow-growth law: deep objects cannot be quickly produced from shallow ones by any deterministic process, nor with much probability by a probabilistic process, but can be pro duced slowly.
findings.bears_on: Suggests a per-block invariant (depth gained relative to theta is at most the block's work) that NCI could aim for; depth is uncomputable, so NCI's cap on novel input is the enforceable proxy.

title: The I/O complexity of Strassen's matrix multiplication with recomputation

findings.claim: The Strassen I/O bound holds even when recomputation is allowed, proved via the Grigoriev flow of the matrix multiplication function rather than graph expansion.
findings.quote: The result generalizes a similar bound previously obtained under the constraint of no-recomputation, that is, that intermediate results cannot be computed more than once.
findings.bears_on: The Grigoriev-flow technique is a property of the function, not of one circuit, so it is the right shape for NCI, where blocks may recompute anything within Gamma gates.

title: Communication Lower Bounds for Statistical Estimation Problems via a Distributed Data Processing Inequality
authors: Mark Braverman, Ankit Garg, Tengyu Ma, Huy L. Nguyen, David P. Woodruff

findings.claim: Distributed sparse linear regression over m machines with n observations each needs total communication Omega(min{n,d} m) to reach minimax error, proved with a distributed strong data processing inequality.
findings.quote: to achieve the statistical minimax error, the total communication is at least $\Omega(\min\{n,d\}m)$, where $n$ is the number of observations that each machine
findings.bears_on: Strong data processing inequalities bound information rather than words, the quantity NCI caps; they could give lower bounds on the novel bits per block for learning tasks independent of the compression scheme.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

title: Communication lower bounds and optimal algorithms for programs that reference arrays -- Part 1
authors: Michael Christ, James Demmel, Nicholas Knight, Thomas Scanlon, Katherine Yelick

findings.claim: Discrete Holder-Brascamp-Lieb inequalities generalize Loomis-Whitney and give communication lower bounds for any loop nest whose array indices are affine in the loop variables.
findings.quote: Using a recent generalization of Loomis’ and Whitney’s result, we generalize this lower bound approach to a much larger class of algorithms, that may have arbitrary numbers of loops and arrays with arbitrary dimensions, as long as the index expressions are affine combinations of loop variables.
findings.bears_on: HBL inequalities with weights let one projection be free and still bound the others, a possible way to bound attention and convolution work per NCI block when only the activation projections are capped.

title: Distributed Verification and Hardness of Distributed Approximation
authors: Atish Das Sarma, Stephan Holzer, Liah Kor, Amos Korman, Danupon Nanongkai, Gopal Pandurangan, et al.

findings.claim: In CONGEST with B-bit messages, many verification problems need Omega(sqrt(n/(B log n)) + D) rounds, proved by reduction from two-party communication complexity across a bottleneck.
findings.quote: We show a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n/(B\log n)}+D)$ for many verification problems in the $B$ model
findings.bears_on: The reduction from set disjointness across a cut is a technique for lower-bounding the novel bits that must cross any NCI block boundary for a given update function.

findings.claim: In distributed settings verification can be harder than computation.
findings.quote: verification is harder than computation in the distributed world!
findings.bears_on: Cautions that per-block checks need not be cheap in a distributed setting; NCI places verification outside the bandwidth-limited model, with committed state and a proof service.

title: Extractor-Based Time-Space Lower Bounds for Learning
authors: Sumegha Garg, Ran Raz, Avishay Tal

findings.claim: For any learning problem whose sample-concept matrix is a (k, l)-extractor with error 2^-r, a learner needs either Omega(k l) memory or 2^Omega(r) samples.
findings.quote: We show that any learning algorithm for the learning problem corresponding to $M$ requires either a memory of size at least $\Omega\left(k\cdot\ell\right)$, or at least $2^{\Omega(r)}$ samples.
findings.bears_on: Generalizes Raz's bound to a broad class of learning problems, so a K-bit cross-block state is a hard bottleneck for any task with extractor structure, not only parities.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

findings.claim: The bound is tight at memory about (log|X|)(log|A|) for many problems.
findings.quote: achieving a tight $\Omega\left((\log|X|)\cdot(\log|A|)\right)$ lower bound on the size of the memory
findings.bears_on: Suggests the memory threshold scales like (bits per sample) x (bits per concept), which for LLM training would be (b_tok x context) x (bits of model), far above K; whether real LLM training has extractor structure is open.

title: I/O complexity: The red-blue pebble game

findings.claim: The red-blue pebble game models a computation's traffic between a small fast memory and a large slow memory, and its S-partition argument cuts the computation into pieces each with a bounded set of inputs, the same shape as an NCI block decomposition.
findings.quote: In this paper, the red-blue pebble game is proposed to model the input-output complexity of algorithms.
findings.bears_on: NCI's block decomposition is an S-partition with the memory bound S replaced by a cap of K novel bits read and a work bound of Gamma gates, so the S-partition counting argument is the natural template for NCI lower bounds.

findings.claim: With fast memory S, the FFT needs Omega(n log n / log S) I/O and classical matrix multiplication needs Omega(n^3 / sqrt(S)), and both bounds are attainable.
findings.quote: with a device of O(S) memory at least Omega(n log n/log S) (or Omega(n-cubed/square root of S), respectively) time is needed for the I/O.

quantities.condition: I/O lower bound for classical n x n matrix multiplication scales as n^3 / S^0.5; S counts all words in fast memory, with no free (committed) operands

findings.bears_on: Gives the classical per-piece work bound (work per piece at most about S^1.5 for matrix multiplication); NCI differs because committed weights are free, which removes one of the three operands from the count.

findings.claim: Hong and Kung's bounds are tight, achieved by blocked decompositions.
findings.quote: All of the lower bounds presented are the best possible in the sense that they are achievable by certain decomposition schemes.
findings.bears_on: Shows that partition-based communication lower bounds can be tight; NCI's slowdown bounds would also want matching attack constructions (decompositions) to show tightness.

title: Communication lower bounds for distributed-memory matrix multiplication
authors: Dror Irony, Sivan Toledo, Alexander Tiskin
venue: Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 64(9)

findings.claim: 2D algorithms, with Theta(n^2/P) memory per processor, communicate O(n^2/P^(1/2)) words per processor, and this is optimal for that memory.
findings.quote: We show that the amount of communication that they perform per processor, O(n 2/P 1/2), is asymptotically optimal for this amount of memory.

quantities.condition: per-processor communication n^2 / P^0.5 with O(n^2/P) memory; conventional Theta(n^3) algorithms only

findings.bears_on: Parallel analogue of a per-block input cap: it bounds the busiest processor, as NCI bounds every block, but counts words rather than novel bits.

findings.claim: 3D algorithms replicate the inputs Theta(P^(1/3)) times and cut communication to Theta(n^2/P^(2/3)) per processor, which is optimal for that memory.
findings.quote: But this allows them to reduce the amount of communication to only Θ(n 2/P 2/3) per processor. We show that this amount of communication is optimal for the amount of memory that is used.
findings.bears_on: Replicating inputs buys less communication; in NCI committed theta is replicated for free, which is the regime where these bounds are weakest.

findings.claim: The bounds cover only classical cubic algorithms, not Strassen-like ones.
findings.quote: Our analysis applies only to conventional matrix-multiplication algorithms. It does not apply to Strassen’s algorithm [23] or other o(n 3) algorithms.
findings.bears_on: Any NCI bound proved by Loomis-Whitney-style counting would not cover an adversary that restructures matrix products bilinearly (Strassen-like); a different technique (expansion, Grigoriev flow, communication complexity) is needed.

findings.claim: The bounds deliberately do not charge for replicating the inputs, the analogue of NCI not charging for committed parameters.
findings.quote: our lower bounds do not even count the communication necessary to perform the replication of input elements!
findings.bears_on: Precedent for leaving initial data distribution free, as NCI does for theta; the bounds then come only from data produced during the computation.

title: An inequality related to the isoperimetric inequality
venue: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55(10)

findings.claim: The volume of a set of unit cubes is bounded by the product of its coordinate projections, with equality for boxes; this is the geometric core of the matrix multiplication communication bounds.
findings.quote: Let S be a set of cubes from a cubical subdivision of n-space; let Si be the set of (n — 1)-cubes obtained by projecting the cubes of S onto the ith coordinate hyperplane.
findings.bears_on: The inequality bounds work per block only if every projection is capped; NCI leaves the weight projection (theta) and the outputs free, so it gives no useful per-block bound by itself.

findings.claim: Boxes aligned with the axes attain the bound, which is why blocked algorithms are optimal.
findings.quote: Note that for w-dimensional intervals with faces parallel to the coordinate hyperplanes, (1) holds with the equality sign.
findings.bears_on: Tightness by boxes suggests the matching NCI attack is a blocked decomposition along the token, layer and weight axes.

title: Fast Learning Requires Good Memory: A Time-Space Lower Bound for Parity Learning

findings.claim: A streaming learner with less than n^2/25 bits of memory needs exponentially many samples to learn an n-bit parity.
findings.quote: We show that any algorithm for parity learning, that uses less than $\frac{n^{2}}{25}$ bits of memory, requires an exponential number of samples.

quantities.condition: derived: n = sqrt(25 K) for K = 2e7 bits (about 47,000 for K = 9e7); applies only if a single thread's K-bit block input is the learner's whole memory between blocks

findings.bears_on: If a training thread carries at most K novel bits from block to block, memory-sample tradeoffs imply exponential (not merely constant-factor) slowdowns for some learning problems with n above about 2e4-5e4.

findings.claim: With quadratic memory the same problem takes O(n) samples by Gaussian elimination, so the gap is caused by the memory bound alone.
findings.quote: Parity learning can be solved in polynomial time, by Gaussian elimination, using $O(n)$ samples and $O(n^{2})$ memory bits.
findings.bears_on: Illustrates the kind of separation a per-block cap could force on learners whose state cannot be compressed, the opposite case to low-U updates such as seed-based fine-tuning.

title: Shuffles and Circuits (On Lower Bounds for Modern Parallel Computation)
authors: Tim Roughgarden, Sergei Vassilvitskii, Joshua R. Wang

findings.claim: The MPC (s-shuffle) model caps each machine's input per round at s bits, smaller than the input, with no communication inside a round.
findings.quote: the "fan-in" of each machine is limited to s bits, where s is smaller than the input size n, and that computation proceeds in synchronized rounds, with no communication between different machines within a round.
findings.bears_on: An MPC machine-round is close to an NCI block (fan-in s ~ K), except that NCI bounds a block's work and gives committed data for free; MPC lower bounds transfer only where those differences do not matter.

findings.claim: Few-round MPC computations are low-degree real polynomials, which gives unconditional round lower bounds.
findings.quote: We prove that computations in our model that use few rounds can be represented as low-degree polynomials over the reals.
findings.bears_on: Polynomial-degree arguments could bound how far information spreads across NCI blocks per round of dependency.

findings.claim: Much stronger generic round lower bounds would separate P from NC1, so unconditional bounds for arbitrary functions are blocked.
findings.quote: Restricting to a polynomial number of machines, we show that asymptotically better lower bounds would separate P from NC 1
findings.bears_on: NCI slowdown bounds cannot come from generic circuit lower bounds; they must use the structure of training (sequential updates, b_w, b_a), as NCI's thread and sharding bounds do.

title: The I/O Complexity of Attention, or How Optimal is Flash Attention?

findings.claim: FlashAttention's N^2 d^2 / M I/O is optimal for every cache size M >= d^2.
findings.quote: an I/O complexity lower bound that matches the upper bound provided by FlashAttention for any values of $M\geq d^{2}$ within any constant factors

quantities.unit: exponent of d in attention I/O
quantities.condition: I/O = Theta(N^2 d^2 / M) for M >= d^2; N = sequence length, d = head dimension

findings.bears_on: Gives a tight data-movement bound for the attention step that dominates long-session inference and training; a template for bounding attention inside an NCI block.

findings.claim: The bound survives fast matrix multiplication because it is proved through a communication complexity protocol, not by counting products.
findings.quote: even if one uses fast matrix multiplication, the above I/O complexity bounds cannot be improved. We do so by introducing a new communication complexity protocol for matrix compression, and connecting communication complexity to I/O complexity.
findings.bears_on: The most directly borrowable technique: NCI already measures information in bits, so a communication complexity lower bound for the update function would transfer to NCI regardless of how the adversary writes the circuit.

title: Information-theoretic lower bounds for distributed statistical estimation with communication constraints
authors: Yuchen Zhang, John C. Duchi, Michael I. Jordan, Martin J. Wainwright

findings.claim: Reaching the centralized minimax rate for d-dimensional estimation from m machines needs about dm/log m bits of communication, even with full interaction.
findings.quote: at least $B\gtrsim\frac{dm}{\log m}$ bits are required for any distributed procedure—even allowing fully interactive communication—to attain the centralized minimax rate.

quantities.unit: bits per coordinate per machine, up to a 1/log m factor
quantities.condition: derived: total dm/log m bits over m machines and d coordinates; Gaussian mean estimation; read as a floor on how far per-shard update messages can be compressed

findings.bears_on: If a training run must split its data over m blocks (each limited to Gamma work), the aggregating blocks must read about dm/log m novel bits, a floor on b_w-like compression of per-shard updates for at least some estimation problems.

findings.claim: Communicating the answer is exponentially cheaper than computing it distributedly: O(d log(mn)) bits describe the solution, yet nearly dm bits must be exchanged.
findings.quote: there is an exponential gap between the number of bits required to communicate the problem solution and the number required to compute it in a distributed manner.
findings.bears_on: NCI's sharding cost uses U, the update's description length; this result says the novel bits needed to compute an update across blocks can far exceed U, so a sharding bound in terms of U may be loose in the adversary's favor.

findings.claim: Each machine individually must send at least d/log m bits.
findings.quote: each machine individually must communicate at least $\frac{d}{\log m}$ bits for a decentralized procedure to match the centralized rate.
findings.bears_on: A per-shard floor, comparable to NCI's per-block cap K: when d/log m exceeds K, a shard's contribution cannot fit in one block's input.
